questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Nature and Characteristics of Groups' refers to.
questions.a: A group is an organised system of two or more interacting, interdependent individuals who share common motives, occupy role relationships and live by norms; this separates it from a crowd that gathers by chance with no structure or belongingness, an audience assembled to watch passively, a mob with one polarised purpose and impulsive homogeneous action, and a team whose members carry complementary skills, shared commitment and mutual accountability that produce positive synergy.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nature and Characteristics of Groups'.
questions.a: A dropped catch by one fielder punishes the whole team - that interdependence, not mere presence at one place, is what makes a family, class or playing set a true group.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Nature and Characteristics of Groups', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: group = two_or_more_members + interdependence + common_motives + roles + norms ; team = group + complementary_skills + mutual_accountability

questions.q: Using the method 'Why People Join Groups', work with: goal_achievement = 25, knowledge_information = 25, psychological_social_needs = 360, security = 40, self_esteem = 120, status = 500. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of join_reasons.
questions.a: 1070 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Why People Join Groups' and work with: goal_achievement = 150, knowledge_information = 500, psychological_social_needs = 400, security = 18, self_esteem = 75, status = 40. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of join_reasons.
questions.a: 1183 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Why People Join Groups' refers to.
questions.a: Group membership pays in several currencies: security against the insecurity of being alone, status borrowed from a group others consider important, self-esteem and positive social identity from prestigious membership, satisfaction of psychological and social needs such as belongingness, attention, love and power, goal achievement that no individual could manage alone, and knowledge and information that widen one's view.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Why People Join Groups'.
questions.a: Because different groups feed different needs, everyone holds several memberships at once - which is why competing demands and expectations press on us.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Why People Join Groups', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: join_reasons = security + status + self_esteem + psychological_social_needs + goal_achievement + knowledge_information

concepts.title: Group Formation: Conditions and Tuckman's Stages

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Group Formation: Conditions and Tuckman's Stages' refers to.
questions.a: Groups arise where contact and interaction are eased by proximity (same colony, school or playground), similarity (consistent, validating company whose views reinforce ours), and common motives or goals such as teaching slum children together. Tuckman then splits development into five stages - forming with uncertainty and excitement, storming with conflict over control and tasks until a leadership hierarchy appears, norming when behaviour norms and positive identity form, performing when the accepted structure drives the goal, and adjourning when a committee disbands after its function ends.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Group Formation: Conditions and Tuckman's Stages'.
questions.a: Groups need not march through the stages neatly - some stages run together, some repeat, and some are skipped entirely.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Group Formation: Conditions and Tuckman's Stages', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: formation_conditions = proximity + similarity + common_motives_goals ; tuckman_stages = forming + storming + norming + performing + adjourning

concepts.title: Group Structure: Roles, Norms, Status and Cohesiveness

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Group Structure: Roles, Norms, Status and Cohesiveness' refers to.
questions.a: As members interact, a structure regularises the group through four elements: roles, the socially defined expectations attached to a position such as son, daughter or team captain; norms, the agreed and enforced standards or unspoken rules of behaviour and belief; status, the relative social position that may be ascribed by seniority or achieved by expertise and hard work; and cohesiveness, the togetherness, we-feeling and mutual attraction that makes members think and act as one unit and holds them in the group.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Group Structure: Roles, Norms, Status and Cohesiveness'.
questions.a: The cricket captain outranks teammates in status though all matter equally; extreme cohesiveness, however, can breed groupthink.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Group Structure: Roles, Norms, Status and Cohesiveness', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: structure_elements = roles + norms + status + cohesiveness ; status = ascribed or achieved

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Groupthink and Its Prevention' refers to.
questions.a: Groupthink, identified by Irving Janis, is the failure of extremely cohesive, like-minded groups whose concern for unanimity overrides realistic appraisal: everyone assumes consensus, dissent stays unspoken for fear of breaking cohesion, the group inflates its own power, and warnings from the real world are minimised - as when President Johnson's circle escalated the Vietnam War against advice. Countermeasures are rewarding critical thinking and disagreement, presenting alternative courses of action, inviting outside experts, and seeking feedback from trusted outsiders.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Groupthink and Its Prevention'.
questions.a: The Vietnam escalation of 1964-67 cost 56000 American and over a million Vietnamese lives - the textbook price of unanimity pressure inside an isolated leadership group.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Groupthink and Its Prevention', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: groupthink_risk = high_cohesion + homogeneity + isolation + no_alternatives + high_cost_decision ; prevention = critical_thinking + alternatives + outside_experts + trusted_feedback

concepts.title: Types of Groups and Tajfel's Minimal Group Paradigm

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Types of Groups and Tajfel's Minimal Group Paradigm' refers to.
questions.a: Groups come in contrasted types: primary groups like family, caste and religion are pre-existing, face-to-face and emotionally warm with impermeable boundaries, while secondary groups such as a political party are joined by choice with impersonal, infrequent ties; formal groups like a university spell out functions, rules and roles, unlike close informal groups; and the ingroup of 'we' is viewed favourably while the outgroup of 'they' is often perceived negatively. Tajfel's minimal group paradigm proved the point: British schoolboys grouped by mere preference for Kandinsky or Klee paintings still distributed money in favour of their own group.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Types of Groups and Tajfel's Minimal Group Paradigm'.
questions.a: Even a flimsy criterion with no past or future is enough to trigger favouritism, though such categories are created by us - and India's composite culture celebrates plurality instead.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Types of Groups and Tajfel's Minimal Group Paradigm', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: type_pairs = primary_vs_secondary + formal_vs_informal + ingroup_vs_outgroup ; minimal_group -> ingroup_favouritism

questions.q: Using the method 'Social Facilitation and Social Loafing', work with: group_size = 2048, output_alone = 30, total_group_output = 45. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of loafing_gap.
questions.a: 29.978 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Social Facilitation and Social Loafing' and work with: group_size = 256, output_alone = 60, total_group_output = 60. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of loafing_gap.
questions.a: 59.7656 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Social Facilitation and Social Loafing' refers to.
questions.a: Social facilitation shows that the presence of others arouses and can lift the performance of someone already good, provided individual effort is evaluated; but when outputs are pooled, as in tug-of-war, individuals work less hard - social loafing, the reduction in individual effort on a collective task that lets members become free riders. Latane's clapping and cheering experiments made the point: total noise rose with group size of two, four and six, yet each participant's noise dropped as the group grew, because responsibility diffuses, individual contribution goes unmeasured, comparison with other groups is absent, coordination is poor, and membership alone does not matter to members. Loafing shrinks when each person's effort is identifiable, pressure to work hard rises, the task gains apparent importance, individual contribution is valued, and cohesiveness strengthens.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Social Facilitation and Social Loafing'.
questions.a: Larger groups divide attention and responsibility, so the per-person share of effort falls even while the group total climbs.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Social Facilitation and Social Loafing', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: effort_per_head = total_group_output / group_size ; loafing_gap = output_alone - effort_per_head

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Group Polarisation' refers to.
questions.a: Group polarisation is the strengthening of a group's initial position through discussion, so that groups take more extreme decisions than individuals would - colleagues may let a bribed employee go scot-free or demand dismissal instead of a proportionate punishment. It happens because like-minded company supplies newer arguments for your view, the visible agreement of others acts as a bandwagon that validates the view as public opinion, and perceived ingroup membership breeds conformity that hardens the stance.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Group Polarisation'.
questions.a: Discussing capital punishment among supporters hardens both pro and anti camps - the danger is that positions may swing from very weak to very strong.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Group Polarisation', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: polarisation = initial_position strengthened by group_discussion ; drivers = new_arguments + bandwagon_validation + ingroup_conformity
